---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/gristlabs/grist-core
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: gristlabs/grist:1.7.17
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: grist
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔⛔ GRIST-CORE HAS NO LOGIN SYSTEM OF ITS OWN, AND ITS FREE ACCOUNT IS THE ADMINISTRATOR ACCOUNT. Read this before anything else. When no OIDC, SAML or forward-auth configuration is present, grist-core falls back to the \"minimal\" login system (app/server/lib/loginSystemHelpers.ts:76-88, MinimalLogin.ts:47-50). That system checks NO credential: a request to the login route calls setUserInSession with a hard-coded profile whose email is GRIST_DEFAULT_EMAIL, or you@example.com when unset (MinimalLogin.ts:10-16,52-56). InstallAdmin.ts:71-80 then treats that same email as the installation administrator. So a plain Grist container on a public hostname is not \"open signup\", it is worse: every visitor is already the owner, and no setting inside Grist closes it. GRIST_FORCE_LOGIN does NOT help, because the login it forces is the one that hands out the account."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: you do, at deploy time, and only because this recipe puts an authenticating proxy in front of Grist. There is no signup form, no install wizard and no registration to close: identity arrives from the proxy. The administrator is fixed by GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL, which you set before the hostname exists, and the only way to reach Grist at all is through HTTP basic auth whose username IS that email. Nothing is claimable by a first visitor because an anonymous request never reaches Grist. Adding a second person is adding a line to the htpasswd file, not an invitation they accept."
  - "⛔ THE AUTH GATE IS THE ENTRY. Deploy BOTH services or do not deploy this at all. The compose in this file publishes ONLY the nginx gate on host port 8080; Grist's own 8484 is not published and is reachable only on the compose network. nginx requires basic auth on every path except /status, and it sets X-Forwarded-User from the authenticated basic-auth username, which OVERWRITES anything the client sent. That last detail is the whole security model: ForwardAuthLogin.ts:52-64 says in terms that Grist will trust whatever is in that header, so a gate that merely adds the header while passing a client-supplied one through is not a gate. The verification script in the body proves both halves, including a request that carries its own X-Forwarded-User."
  - "⛔ FORWARD AUTH, MODE 2: GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER=X-Forwarded-User plus GRIST_IGNORE_SESSION=true. With GRIST_IGNORE_SESSION set, Grist skips its session cookie entirely and reads the header on EVERY request (ForwardAuthLogin.ts:52-64, Authorizer.ts:353-362), which is what makes the gate total rather than login-time only. The user record is created from the header profile on first sight. Consequences to state plainly to the user: logging out is a browser basic-auth concern, not a Grist one, and the basic-auth username must be a real email address because Grist uses it as the account identity."
  - "⛔ DATABASE, AND IT HAS A TWIST THE OTHER ENTRIES DO NOT HAVE. dbUtils.ts:168-178 defaults TYPEORM_TYPE to sqlite, and Dockerfile:192 sets TYPEORM_DATABASE=/persist/home.sqlite3 inside the image. So an unwired deploy comes up perfectly healthy on a container-local SQLite file. The twist: setting TYPEORM_TYPE=postgres and forgetting TYPEORM_DATABASE does NOT fall back sensibly, it asks Postgres for a database literally named /persist/home.sqlite3. Set all five: TYPEORM_TYPE=postgres, TYPEORM_HOST=${PGHOST}, TYPEORM_PORT=${PGPORT}, TYPEORM_DATABASE=${PGDATABASE}, TYPEORM_USERNAME=${PGUSER}, TYPEORM_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]}. deploy_compose only APPENDS those PG* variables to the project .env, it never edits your compose, so the compose has to interpolate them itself, which the one in this file does."
  - "PROVE THE DATABASE WIRING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, because a green page proves nothing about which database it landed in. Positive half first, since it is what tells you your command ran at all: `sudo docker compose exec -T grist ls -la /persist` must list docs/ and must NOT list home.sqlite3. Then the other half, from the app VM: `sudo docker compose exec -T grist printenv TYPEORM_TYPE TYPEORM_DATABASE` must print postgres and your database name. If the first command errors, the second one's output means nothing. Note the VM runs docker, not podman."
  - "⛔⛔ POSTGRES DOES NOT HOLD YOUR SPREADSHEETS. This is the single most misread thing about self-hosted Grist. The managed Postgres is the HOME database: users, orgs, workspaces, document metadata, ACL rules and API keys. Every actual document is a .grist file (itself a SQLite database) under GRIST_DATA_DIR, which Dockerfile:184 sets to /persist/docs, and attachments live beside it. Mount a volume on /persist or a redeploy leaves you with a Grist that lists every document and has none of them. Prove it after boot with `sudo docker compose exec -T grist ls /persist/docs` and by confirming /persist appears in `sudo docker inspect -f '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Destination}} {{end}}' <container>`. Object storage (MinIO or S3) is the only way to move documents off the volume, and this recipe does not set it up."
  - "⛔ SET GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR=gvisor. Formulas in Grist are Python, and grist-core's DEFAULT IS UNSANDBOXED: ICreate.ts:183-184 passes \"unsandboxed\" as the default flavor and NSandbox.ts:1357-1358 only overrides it from GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR. Unsandboxed means anyone who can edit a formula runs arbitrary Python inside the container, with its filesystem and its network. The official image already ships runsc and sets GVISOR_FLAGS=\"-unprivileged -ignore-cgroups\" (Dockerfile:189), and sandbox/run.sh:5-16 pre-flights runsc and EXITS 1 with the flags in the message when it cannot run, so this fails closed and loudly rather than quietly downgrading. If it does fail on your host, that is a decision to put to the user, not a value to quietly drop."
  - "SET GRIST_SESSION_SECRET AND REUSE IT ON EVERY REDEPLOY. This is the entry's version of the secret every other app in this library has, and it is honestly the mildest one: ICreate.ts:47-57,187-189 falls back to a constant that is published in the open-source tree, so an unset secret means your cookies are signed with a value every reader of the repo has. Upstream's own comment beside it says the only consequence of changing the secret is that existing sessions are invalidated. Generate one alphanumeric value, store it with the deployment, and pass the same one back on every redeploy."
  - "APP_HOME_URL MUST BE THE FINAL PUBLIC URL, and it is needed at deploy time rather than after. Grist builds redirects and links from it. Generate the dname yourself, in full `grist-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud` form, before creating anything, and set APP_HOME_URL=https://<that name>. The image already sets GRIST_SERVE_SAME_ORIGIN=true and GRIST_ORG_IN_PATH=true, so URLs look like /o/docs/...; GRIST_SINGLE_ORG=<team> is the documented alternative if the user wants a single named team instead."
  - "PORT 8080 IS THE GATE, NOT GRIST. Pass port 8080 to deploy_compose, which is the nginx container. Grist itself listens on 8484 (Dockerfile:194; stubs/app/server/server.ts:63 lets PORT override it) and must stay unpublished. Health probe for humans: GET /status, the one path the gate leaves open, which answers with Grist's own \"is alive\" line and nothing else."
  - "DELETE THESE FROM ANY UPSTREAM EXAMPLE YOU ARE TEMPTED TO COPY. None of the five files under docker-compose-examples/ is deployable here. Drop traefik and authelia (redu terminates TLS in front of you), drop the bundled postgres (you get a managed one), drop redis (Grist needs it only for multi-server installs) and drop minio plus its minio-setup helper (only wanted if you move documents into object storage). What is left is one service, which is why this file ships a purpose-written compose instead."
  - "PIN FROM THE REGISTRY, AND NOTE THE TAG SHAPE. GitHub releases are named v1.7.17; the Docker Hub tags have NO leading v. gristlabs/grist:1.7.17 resolves to the same digest as stable, 1 and 1.7 (checked 2026-08-17, published 2026-07-29). Every upstream example compose says gristlabs/grist:latest; replace it with the pinned tag before you deploy anything, so a redeploy cannot cross a release."
  - "REGISTRATION AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT: there is none to close, because Grist has no signup. Access is exactly the set of lines in the htpasswd file. Two defaults are still worth knowing: GRIST_ORG_CREATION_ANYONE defaults true (gristSettings.ts:143-150), so any authenticated user can create new teams, and GRIST_ANON_PLAYGROUND inherits that default, so an unauthenticated visitor could create throwaway documents if the gate were ever removed. The compose sets GRIST_ANON_PLAYGROUND=false, which is belt and braces behind the gate."
  - "NGINX RESOLVES THE UPSTREAM NAME ONCE, AT STARTUP. If you later recreate only the grist container, restart the gate container too, or it will keep proxying to an address that no longer exists. `sudo docker compose restart auth` is the whole fix. Equally, if the gate fails to start it fails CLOSED: a missing htpasswd file gives 500s, never open access."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> generate the dname -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (GBP 0.0452/hr, about GBP 33 a month, inside the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> prepare_upload with the two-service compose, the nginx config and the generated htpasswd -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2', port 8080. ⚠️ plan_deploy will want to upsize a compose stack to m1.large; pass flavor_id '3' explicitly to hold m1.medium, and always pass db_flavor_id or the database VM defaults to the app flavor and doubles the bill."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source and the repo is a monorepo you do not need. Write the compose, auth/nginx.conf and auth/htpasswd locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. The htpasswd line is generated at deploy time with `openssl passwd -apr1 -stdin` reading the password from STDIN, never from argv, because an argument is visible in ps to every user on the machine."
  - "LICENCE: Apache License 2.0, read from LICENSE.txt in the repo rather than from third-party metadata. Nothing to reason about for a self-hoster: you deploy it into your own account and run it yourself. Apache-2.0 grants no trademark rights, so do not rebrand and redistribute under the Grist name, and keep the NOTICE and licence text with any copy you pass on."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres, which keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr; delete_database removes it. ⚠️ Read the storage split above before you delete anything: the home database survives in Postgres while every actual document lives on the app VM's volume and goes with the deployment. Export anything you care about from Grist first."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. Checked the README, the Dockerfile and all five compose examples: there is no RAM figure anywhere. m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is reasoning from the shape of the thing, a Node server plus one Python process per open document plus gvisor overhead, and 40 GB of flavor disk for documents and attachments. Disk is the constraint that bites later, since growing it is a volume resize rather than a redeploy. Measure both on your run and write the numbers back here rather than repeating this paragraph."
---

# Self-host Grist on redu

Grist is a spreadsheet with a relational spine: real tables, real references, Python formulas and
row-level access rules. This deploys it from the official image onto one VM, behind an

## Read this before you deploy: Grist has no login system

This is not a hardening note, it is the reason the recipe has two containers.

grist-core ships without any password login. When no identity provider is configured it falls back
to a "minimal" login system that checks no credential at all: visiting the login route signs you in
as a single hard-coded account, and that same account is the installation administrator. On a
public hostname that means every visitor is already the owner, and no setting inside Grist changes
it.

Upstream's answer is to put an authenticating proxy in front, and it ships examples doing exactly
that with Traefik. redu already terminates TLS, so this recipe uses the same mechanism with a small
nginx container instead: basic auth on every path, and the authenticated username passed to Grist
in a header it trusts.

That gives a clean answer to the question every entry in this library has to answer. **You become
the administrator at deploy time**, because `GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL` is set before the hostname exists
and the gate only lets that identity through. There is no signup form and no window to close.

And `auth/nginx.conf`. The line that matters is `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User $remote_user`:
it replaces whatever the client sent, which is what stops the header being spoofed.

```nginx
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name _;
    client_max_body_size 512m;

    # Liveness only. Grist answers here with its own "is alive" line and nothing else.
    location = /status {
        proxy_pass http://grist:8484/status;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User "";
    }

    location / {
        auth_basic           "Grist";
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/htpasswd;

        proxy_pass http://grist:8484;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User  $remote_user;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade           $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection        $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
    }
}
```

Setting a header to `""` in nginx means it is not sent at all, so the `/status` location strips any
client-supplied identity rather than forwarding it.

## Building the htpasswd line

The username must be the email you want to own the instance, because Grist uses it as the account
identity. Nothing here puts the password in `ps`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Write auth/htpasswd for the gate. Run it in the upload directory before prepare_upload.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com ./make-htpasswd.sh
set -eu
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email that should own this Grist}"

mkdir -p auth
# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in a shell, a URL or JSON.
GATE_PASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)

# -stdin keeps it out of the process list; every user on the box can read argv.
hash=$(printf '%s' "$GATE_PASS" | openssl passwd -apr1 -stdin)
printf '%s:%s\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$hash" > auth/htpasswd

echo "Gate user: $GATE_EMAIL"
echo "Gate secret (shown once, store it in your manager now):"
printf '%s\n' "$GATE_PASS"
echo
echo "Set GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL to $GATE_EMAIL in the compose .env, or the gate will let you in"
echo "as a user who is not the installation administrator."
```

## Proving the gate is real

Run this once the deploy reports ready. A gate you have not tested is a gate you are guessing
about, and the failure mode is an instance where every visitor is the owner.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove the Grist gate is in front, cannot be bypassed by a spoofed header, and identifies you.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com GATE_SECRET=[REDACTED:value] ./verify-grist.sh grist-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = gated and working, 1 = NOT gated, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-grist.sh <host>}"
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email you deployed with}"
: "${GATE_SECRET:[REDACTED:value] GATE_SECRET to the gate secret}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE THE WHOLE SCRIPT ON PROOF THAT GRIST IS ANSWERING. Everything below is vacuous
#    against an error page, and redu's hostname answers 502 for the first minutes.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/status" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/status")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; this is NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q "is alive" "$TMP/status"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status returned 200 but not Grist's own body." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as gated." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# 2. Anonymous must be refused. 401 is the POSITIVE result here, not a problem.
anon=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$anon" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request to / answered $anon, expected 401." >&2
  echo "The gate is not in front of Grist. Anyone loading this URL is already the administrator." >&2
  echo "Do not leave this instance running." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 3. And it must not be bypassable by sending the trusted header yourself.
spoof=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "X-Forwarded-User: someone-else@example.org" "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$spoof" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: a request carrying its own X-Forwarded-User answered $spoof, expected 401." >&2
  echo "nginx is not overwriting the header, so identity is client-controlled." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. The positive half, which is what proves the two 401s above mean anything at all:
#    with the gate credentials, Grist must report YOU as the signed-in user.
printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$GATE_SECRET" > "$TMP/curlrc"
me=$(curl -sS -K "$TMP/curlrc" -o "$TMP/me" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/profile/user")
if [ "$me" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: authenticated /api/profile/user answered $me." >&2
  echo "  A 404 means the endpoint moved: probe for the live route rather than assuming this one," >&2
  echo "  and do not read a 404 as a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -qi "$GATE_EMAIL" "$TMP/me"; then
  echo "FAIL: authenticated, but Grist does not report $GATE_EMAIL as the user." >&2
  echo "The forward-auth header is not reaching Grist. Check GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "OK: /status alive, anonymous 401, spoofed header 401, Grist reports $GATE_EMAIL."
echo "Two things left for a human: open a document and check a formula evaluates (that is the"
echo "Python sandbox), and confirm /persist is a mounted volume, not container-local disk."
```

## The three that actually break it

**No login system.** Covered above, and it is the reason for the second container. A single-container
Grist on a public URL hands ownership to whoever loads it.

**The database that is not your data.** Postgres holds accounts, orgs and metadata. Your actual
documents are `.grist` files under `/persist/docs`. Without the volume, a redeploy leaves a Grist
that lists everything and has nothing.

**The sandbox default.** Formulas are Python, and grist-core defaults to running them unsandboxed
inside the container. `GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR=gvisor` uses the runsc that the official image already
ships, and it fails loudly if it cannot.

Setting a header to `""` in nginx means it is not sent at all, so the `/status` location strips any
client-supplied identity rather than forwarding it.

## Building the htpasswd line

The username must be the email you want to own the instance, because Grist uses it as the account
identity. Nothing here puts the password in `ps`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Write auth/htpasswd for the gate. Run it in the upload directory before prepare_upload.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com ./make-htpasswd.sh
set -eu
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email that should own this Grist}"

mkdir -p auth
# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in a shell, a URL or JSON.
GATE_PASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)

# -stdin keeps it out of the process list; every user on the box can read argv.
hash=$(printf '%s' "$GATE_PASS" | openssl passwd -apr1 -stdin)
printf '%s:%s\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$hash" > auth/htpasswd

echo "Gate user: $GATE_EMAIL"
echo "Gate secret (shown once, store it in your manager now):"
printf '%s\n' "$GATE_PASS"
echo
echo "Set GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL to $GATE_EMAIL in the compose .env, or the gate will let you in"
echo "as a user who is not the installation administrator."
```

## Proving the gate is real

Run this once the deploy reports ready. A gate you have not tested is a gate you are guessing
about, and the failure mode is an instance where every visitor is the owner.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove the Grist gate is in front, cannot be bypassed by a spoofed header, and identifies you.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com GATE_SECRET=[REDACTED:value] ./verify-grist.sh grist-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = gated and working, 1 = NOT gated, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-grist.sh <host>}"
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email you deployed with}"
: "${GATE_SECRET:[REDACTED:value] GATE_SECRET to the gate secret}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE THE WHOLE SCRIPT ON PROOF THAT GRIST IS ANSWERING. Everything below is vacuous
#    against an error page, and redu's hostname answers 502 for the first minutes.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/status" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/status")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; this is NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q "is alive" "$TMP/status"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status returned 200 but not Grist's own body." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as gated." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# 2. Anonymous must be refused. 401 is the POSITIVE result here, not a problem.
anon=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$anon" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request to / answered $anon, expected 401." >&2
  echo "The gate is not in front of Grist. Anyone loading this URL is already the administrator." >&2
  echo "Do not leave this instance running." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 3. And it must not be bypassable by sending the trusted header yourself.
spoof=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "X-Forwarded-User: someone-else@example.org" "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$spoof" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: a request carrying its own X-Forwarded-User answered $spoof, expected 401." >&2
  echo "nginx is not overwriting the header, so identity is client-controlled." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. The positive half, which is what proves the two 401s above mean anything at all:
#    with the gate credentials, Grist must report YOU as the signed-in user.
printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$GATE_SECRET" > "$TMP/curlrc"
me=$(curl -sS -K "$TMP/curlrc" -o "$TMP/me" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/profile/user")
if [ "$me" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: authenticated /api/profile/user answered $me." >&2
  echo "  A 404 means the endpoint moved: probe for the live route rather than assuming this one," >&2
  echo "  and do not read a 404 as a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -qi "$GATE_EMAIL" "$TMP/me"; then
  echo "FAIL: authenticated, but Grist does not report $GATE_EMAIL as the user." >&2
  echo "The forward-auth header is not reaching Grist. Check GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "OK: /status alive, anonymous 401, spoofed header 401, Grist reports $GATE_EMAIL."
echo "Two things left for a human: open a document and check a formula evaluates (that is the"
echo "Python sandbox), and confirm /persist is a mounted volume, not container-local disk."
```

## The three that actually break it

**No login system.** Covered above, and it is the reason for the second container. A single-container
Grist on a public URL hands ownership to whoever loads it.

**The database that is not your data.** Postgres holds accounts, orgs and metadata. Your actual
documents are `.grist` files under `/persist/docs`. Without the volume, a redeploy leaves a Grist
that lists everything and has nothing.

**The sandbox default.** Formulas are Python, and grist-core defaults to running them unsandboxed
inside the container. `GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR=gvisor` uses the runsc that the official image already
ships, and it fails loudly if it cannot.

# Self-host Grist on redu

Grist is a spreadsheet with a relational spine: real tables, real references, Python formulas and
row-level access rules. This deploys it from the official image onto one VM, behind an
authenticating gate, with a managed Postgres beside it and a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Grist** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM.
- **An nginx auth gate** in front of it, on port 8080, which is the only published port.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding accounts, orgs and document metadata.
- A volume on `/persist`, which is where the documents themselves live.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Grist on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this before you deploy: Grist has no login system

This is not a hardening note, it is the reason the recipe has two containers.

grist-core ships without any password login. When no identity provider is configured it falls back
to a "minimal" login system that checks no credential at all: visiting the login route signs you in
as a single hard-coded account, and that same account is the installation administrator. On a
public hostname that means every visitor is already the owner, and no setting inside Grist changes
it.

Upstream's answer is to put an authenticating proxy in front, and it ships examples doing exactly
that with Traefik. redu already terminates TLS, so this recipe uses the same mechanism with a small
nginx container instead: basic auth on every path, and the authenticated username passed to Grist
in a header it trusts.

That gives a clean answer to the question every entry in this library has to answer. **You become
the administrator at deploy time**, because `GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL` is set before the hostname exists
and the gate only lets that identity through. There is no signup form and no window to close.

And `auth/nginx.conf`. The line that matters is `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User $remote_user`:
it replaces whatever the client sent, which is what stops the header being spoofed.

```nginx
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name _;
    client_max_body_size 512m;

    # Liveness only. Grist answers here with its own "is alive" line and nothing else.
    location = /status {
        proxy_pass http://grist:8484/status;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User "";
    }

    location / {
        auth_basic           "Grist";
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/htpasswd;

        proxy_pass http://grist:8484;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User  $remote_user;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade           $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection        $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
    }
}
```

Setting a header to `""` in nginx means it is not sent at all, so the `/status` location strips any
client-supplied identity rather than forwarding it.

## Building the htpasswd line

The username must be the email you want to own the instance, because Grist uses it as the account
identity. Nothing here puts the password in `ps`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Write auth/htpasswd for the gate. Run it in the upload directory before prepare_upload.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com ./make-htpasswd.sh
set -eu
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email that should own this Grist}"

mkdir -p auth
# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in a shell, a URL or JSON.
GATE_PASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)

# -stdin keeps it out of the process list; every user on the box can read argv.
hash=$(printf '%s' "$GATE_PASS" | openssl passwd -apr1 -stdin)
printf '%s:%s\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$hash" > auth/htpasswd

echo "Gate user: $GATE_EMAIL"
echo "Gate secret (shown once, store it in your manager now):"
printf '%s\n' "$GATE_PASS"
echo
echo "Set GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL to $GATE_EMAIL in the compose .env, or the gate will let you in"
echo "as a user who is not the installation administrator."

## Proving the gate is real

Run this once the deploy reports ready. A gate you have not tested is a gate you are guessing
about, and the failure mode is an instance where every visitor is the owner.

#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com GATE_SECRET=[REDACTED:value] ./verify-grist.sh grist-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = gated and working, 1 = NOT gated, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE THE WHOLE SCRIPT ON PROOF THAT GRIST IS ANSWERING. Everything below is vacuous
#    against an error page, and redu's hostname answers 502 for the first minutes.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/status" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/status")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; this is NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q "is alive" "$TMP/status"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status returned 200 but not Grist's own body." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as gated." >&2

  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request to / answered $anon, expected 401." >&2
  echo "The gate is not in front of Grist. Anyone loading this URL is already the administrator." >&2
  echo "Do not leave this instance running." >&2

if [ "$spoof" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: a request carrying its own X-Forwarded-User answered $spoof, expected 401." >&2
  echo "nginx is not overwriting the header, so identity is client-controlled." >&2

cat > verify-grist.sh <<'SH'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove the Grist gate is in front, cannot be bypassed by a spoofed header, and identifies you.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com GATE_SECRET=[REDACTED:value] ./verify-grist.sh grist-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = gated and working, 1 = NOT gated, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-grist.sh <host>}"
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email you deployed with}"
: "${GATE_SECRET:[REDACTED:value] GATE_SECRET to the gate secret}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE THE WHOLE SCRIPT ON PROOF THAT GRIST IS ANSWERING. Everything below is vacuous
#    against an error page, and redu's hostname answers 502 for the first minutes.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/status" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/status")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; this is NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q "is alive" "$TMP/status"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status returned 200 but not Grist's own body." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as gated." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# 2. Anonymous must be refused. 401 is the POSITIVE result here, not a problem.
anon=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$anon" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request to / answered $anon, expected 401." >&2
  echo "The gate is not in front of Grist. Anyone loading this URL is already the administrator." >&2
  echo "Do not leave this instance running." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 3. And it must not be bypassable by sending the trusted header yourself.
spoof=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "X-Forwarded-User: someone-else@example.org" "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$spoof" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: a request carrying its own X-Forwarded-User answered $spoof, expected 401." >&2
  echo "nginx is not overwriting the header, so identity is client-controlled." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. The positive half, which is what proves the two 401s above mean anything at all:
#    with the gate credentials, Grist must report YOU as the signed-in user.
printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$GATE_SECRET" > "$TMP/curlrc"
me=$(curl -sS -K "$TMP/curlrc" -o "$TMP/me" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/profile/user")
if [ "$me" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: authenticated /api/profile/user answered $me." >&2
  echo "  A 404 means the endpoint moved: probe for the live route rather than assuming this one," >&2
  echo "  and do not read a 404 as a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -qi "$GATE_EMAIL" "$TMP/me"; then
  echo "FAIL: authenticated, but Grist does not report $GATE_EMAIL as the user." >&2
  echo "The forward-auth header is not reaching Grist. Check GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "OK: /status alive, anonymous 401, spoofed header 401, Grist reports $GATE_EMAIL."
echo "Two things left for a human: open a document and check a formula evaluates (that is the"
echo "Python sandbox), and confirm /persist is a mounted volume, not container-local disk."
SH
chmod +x verify-grist.sh && echo "verify-grist.sh written"

content.text:
Found it — and it's a genuine gap in the recipe's nginx config, not a deploy mistake.

nginx passes the client's `Authorization: Basic ...` header straight through to Grist. Grist's API parses that header expecting an API key and rejects anything that isn't `Bearer`:

```
{"error":"Bad request: unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'"}
```

So the gate authenticates you correctly (nginx logged `$remote_user`), then Grist 401s on the leftover Basic credentials. The fix is one line: strip `Authorization` before proxying, since forward-auth identity travels in `X-Forwarded-User` and doesn't need it.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import re
p='auth/nginx.conf'
s=open(p).read()
old='''        proxy_pass http://grist:8484;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;'''
new='''        proxy_pass http://grist:8484;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        # Grist parses Authorization itself and only accepts `Bearer <api-key>`, so the gate's
        # own `Basic` credentials reach it as a malformed API key and every request 401s with
        # "unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'". Identity travels in
        # X-Forwarded-User, so the header has no job past this point: drop it.
        proxy_set_header Authorization    "";
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;'''
assert old in s, "anchor not found"
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("patched")
PY

API clients authenticate as the basic-auth user and inherit that identity, which is what you want anyway. # Self-host Grist on redu

Grist is a spreadsheet with a relational spine: real tables, real references, Python formulas and
row-level access rules. This deploys it from the official image onto one VM, behind an
authenticating gate, with a managed Postgres beside it and a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Grist** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM.
- **An nginx auth gate** in front of it, on port 8080, which is the only published port.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding accounts, orgs and document metadata.
- A volume on `/persist`, which is where the documents themselves live.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Grist on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this before you deploy: Grist has no login system

This is not a hardening note, it is the reason the recipe has two containers.

grist-core ships without any password login. When no identity provider is configured it falls back
to a "minimal" login system that checks no credential at all: visiting the login route signs you in
as a single hard-coded account, and that same account is the installation administrator. On a
public hostname that means every visitor is already the owner, and no setting inside Grist changes
it.

Upstream's answer is to put an authenticating proxy in front, and it ships examples doing exactly
that with Traefik. redu already terminates TLS, so this recipe uses the same mechanism with a small
nginx container instead: basic auth on every path, and the authenticated username passed to Grist
in a header it trusts.

That gives a clean answer to the question every entry in this library has to answer. **You become
the administrator at deploy time**, because `GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL` is set before the hostname exists
and the gate only lets that identity through. There is no signup form and no window to close.

## The compose

Two services. Grist's own port is deliberately not published.

  auth:
    image: nginx:1.30.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      - grist
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./auth/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
      - ./auth/htpasswd:«REDACTED:assigned:1749190f»

  grist:
    image: gristlabs/grist:1.7.17
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      APP_HOME_URL: ${APP_HOME_URL}
      GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER: X-Forwarded-User
      GRIST_IGNORE_SESSION: "true"

      TYPEORM_PORT: ${PGPORT}
      TYPEORM_DATABASE: ${PGDATABASE}

```

And `auth/nginx.conf`. Two lines carry the whole security model. `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User
$remote_user` replaces whatever the client sent, which is what stops the header being spoofed. And
`proxy_set_header Authorization ""` drops the basic-auth credentials before they reach Grist, which
parses that header itself and rejects anything that is not a Bearer API key — without it every
authenticated request 401s while the gate looks perfectly healthy.

```nginx
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name _;
    client_max_body_size 512m;

    # Liveness only. Grist answers here with its own "is alive" line and nothing else.
    location = /status {
        proxy_pass http://grist:8484/status;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User "";
    }

    location / {
        auth_basic           "Grist";
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/htpasswd;

        proxy_pass http://grist:8484;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        # Grist parses Authorization itself and only accepts `Bearer <api-key>`, so the gate's
        # own `Basic` credentials reach it as a malformed API key and every request 401s with
        # "unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'". Identity travels in
        # X-Forwarded-User, so the header has no job past this point: drop it.
        proxy_set_header Authorization    "";
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User  $remote_user;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade           $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection        $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
    }
}
```

Setting a header to `""` in nginx means it is not sent at all, so the `/status` location strips any
client-supplied identity rather than forwarding it, and the `location /` block strips the basic-auth
credentials rather than passing them upstream.

## Building the htpasswd line

The username must be the email you want to own the instance, because Grist uses it as the account
identity. Nothing here puts the password in `ps`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Write auth/htpasswd for the gate. Run it in the upload directory before prepare_upload.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com ./make-htpasswd.sh
set -eu
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email that should own this Grist}"

mkdir -p auth
# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in a shell, a URL or JSON.
GATE_PASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)

# -stdin keeps it out of the process list; every user on the box can read argv.
hash=$(printf '%s' "$GATE_PASS" | openssl passwd -apr1 -stdin)
printf '%s:%s\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$hash" > auth/htpasswd

echo "Gate user: $GATE_EMAIL"
echo "Gate secret (shown once, store it in your manager now):"
printf '%s\n' "$GATE_PASS"
echo
echo "Set GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL to $GATE_EMAIL in the compose .env, or the gate will let you in"
echo "as a user who is not the installation administrator."
```

## Proving the gate is real

Run this once the deploy reports ready. A gate you have not tested is a gate you are guessing
about, and the failure mode is an instance where every visitor is the owner.

Step 4 is not decoration. It is the step that caught the Authorization-header bug on the first real
run of this recipe, in a deploy where steps 1 to 3 all passed.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove the Grist gate is in front, cannot be bypassed by a spoofed header, and identifies you.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com GATE_SECRET=[REDACTED:value] ./verify-grist.sh grist-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = gated and working, 1 = NOT gated, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-grist.sh <host>}"
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email you deployed with}"
: "${GATE_SECRET:[REDACTED:value] GATE_SECRET to the gate secret}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE THE WHOLE SCRIPT ON PROOF THAT GRIST IS ANSWERING. Everything below is vacuous
#    against an error page, and redu's hostname answers 502 for the first minutes.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/status" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/status")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; this is NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q "is alive" "$TMP/status"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status returned 200 but not Grist's own body." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as gated." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# 2. Anonymous must be refused. 401 is the POSITIVE result here, not a problem.
anon=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$anon" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request to / answered $anon, expected 401." >&2
  echo "The gate is not in front of Grist. Anyone loading this URL is already the administrator." >&2
  echo "Do not leave this instance running." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 3. And it must not be bypassable by sending the trusted header yourself.
spoof=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "X-Forwarded-User: someone-else@example.org" "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$spoof" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: a request carrying its own X-Forwarded-User answered $spoof, expected 401." >&2
  echo "nginx is not overwriting the header, so identity is client-controlled." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. The positive half, which is what proves the two 401s above mean anything at all:
#    with the gate credentials, Grist must report YOU as the signed-in user.
#    A 401 HERE, with steps 1-3 passing, is the Authorization-header bug: nginx is forwarding
#    the basic-auth credentials and Grist is rejecting them as a malformed API key. Confirm with
#    `curl -u "$GATE_EMAIL:$GATE_SECRET" https://$HOST/api/profile/user`, which prints
#    "unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'". Fix: proxy_set_header Authorization "".
printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$GATE_SECRET" > "$TMP/curlrc"
me=$(curl -sS -K "$TMP/curlrc" -o "$TMP/me" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/profile/user")
if [ "$me" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: authenticated /api/profile/user answered $me." >&2
  echo "  A 404 means the endpoint moved: probe for the live route rather than assuming this one," >&2
  echo "  and do not read a 404 as a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -qi "$GATE_EMAIL" "$TMP/me"; then
  echo "FAIL: authenticated, but Grist does not report $GATE_EMAIL as the user." >&2
  echo "The forward-auth header is not reaching Grist. Check GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "OK: /status alive, anonymous 401, spoofed header 401, Grist reports $GATE_EMAIL."
echo "Two things left for a human: open a document and check a formula evaluates (that is the"
echo "Python sandbox), and confirm /persist is a mounted volume, not container-local disk."
```

## The three that actually break it

**No login system.** Covered above, and it is the reason for the second container. A single-container
Grist on a public URL hands ownership to whoever loads it.

**The database that is not your data.** Postgres holds accounts, orgs and metadata. Your actual
documents are `.grist` files under `/persist/docs`. Without the volume, a redeploy leaves a Grist
that lists everything and has nothing.

**The sandbox default.** Formulas are Python, and grist-core defaults to running them unsandboxed
inside the container. `GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR=gvisor` uses the runsc that the official image already
ships, and it fails loudly if it cannot.

  `Authorization` header to Grist, which parses it as an API key and 401s everything with
  "unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'" — the gate looked healthy and logged the
  right `$remote_user` while Grist refused every request. `proxy_set_header Authorization ""` fixed
  it. Everything else in the entry held: gvisor logged `gvisor check ok` and a Python formula

  metadata went to Postgres, and the spoofed-header request was refused. Idle footprint measured at

# Self-host Grist on redu

Grist is a spreadsheet with a relational spine: real tables, real references, Python formulas and
row-level access rules. This deploys it from the official image onto one VM, behind an
authenticating gate, with a managed Postgres beside it and a public HTTPS URL.

## What this deploys

- **Grist** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM.
- **An nginx auth gate** in front of it, on port 8080, which is the only published port.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, holding accounts, orgs and document metadata.
- A volume on `/persist`, which is where the documents themselves live.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Grist on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Read this before you deploy: Grist has no login system

This is not a hardening note, it is the reason the recipe has two containers.

grist-core ships without any password login. When no identity provider is configured it falls back
to a "minimal" login system that checks no credential at all: visiting the login route signs you in
as a single hard-coded account, and that same account is the installation administrator. On a
public hostname that means every visitor is already the owner, and no setting inside Grist changes
it.

Upstream's answer is to put an authenticating proxy in front, and it ships examples doing exactly
that with Traefik. redu already terminates TLS, so this recipe uses the same mechanism with a small
nginx container instead: basic auth on every path, and the authenticated username passed to Grist
in a header it trusts.

That gives a clean answer to the question every entry in this library has to answer. **You become
the administrator at deploy time**, because `GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL` is set before the hostname exists
and the gate only lets that identity through. There is no signup form and no window to close.

## The compose

Two services. Grist's own port is deliberately not published.

```yaml
services:
  auth:
    image: nginx:1.30.4-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      - grist
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./auth/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
      - ./auth/htpasswd:«REDACTED:assigned:1749190f»

  grist:
    image: gristlabs/grist:1.7.17
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      APP_HOME_URL: ${APP_HOME_URL}
      GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER: X-Forwarded-User
      GRIST_IGNORE_SESSION: "true"
      GRIST_FORCE_LOGIN: "true"
      GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL: ${GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL}
      GRIST_DEFAULT_EMAIL: ${GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL}
      GRIST_ANON_PLAYGROUND: "false"
      GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR: gvisor
      GRIST_SESSION_SECRET: [REDACTED:value]}
      TYPEORM_TYPE: postgres
      TYPEORM_HOST: ${PGHOST}
      TYPEORM_PORT: ${PGPORT}
      TYPEORM_DATABASE: ${PGDATABASE}

And `auth/nginx.conf`. Two lines carry the whole security model. `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User
$remote_user` replaces whatever the client sent, which is what stops the header being spoofed. And
`proxy_set_header Authorization ""` drops the basic-auth credentials before they reach Grist, which
parses that header itself and rejects anything that is not a Bearer API key — without it every
authenticated request 401s while the gate looks perfectly healthy.

```nginx
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name _;
    client_max_body_size 512m;

    # Liveness only. Grist answers here with its own "is alive" line and nothing else.
    location = /status {
        proxy_pass http://grist:8484/status;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User "";
    }

    location / {
        auth_basic           "Grist";
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/htpasswd;

        proxy_pass http://grist:8484;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        # Grist parses Authorization itself and only accepts `Bearer <api-key>`, so the gate's
        # own `Basic` credentials reach it as a malformed API key and every request 401s with
        # "unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'". Identity travels in
        # X-Forwarded-User, so the header has no job past this point: drop it.
        proxy_set_header Authorization    "";
        proxy_set_header Host              $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP         $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User  $remote_user;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade           $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection        $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_send_timeout 3600s;
    }
}
```

Setting a header to `""` in nginx means it is not sent at all, so the `/status` location strips any
client-supplied identity rather than forwarding it, and the `location /` block strips the basic-auth
credentials rather than passing them upstream.

## Building the htpasswd line

The username must be the email you want to own the instance, because Grist uses it as the account
identity. Nothing here puts the password in `ps`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Write auth/htpasswd for the gate. Run it in the upload directory before prepare_upload.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com ./make-htpasswd.sh
set -eu
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email that should own this Grist}"

mkdir -p auth
# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in a shell, a URL or JSON.
GATE_PASS=[REDACTED:value] tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 24)

# -stdin keeps it out of the process list; every user on the box can read argv.
hash=$(printf '%s' "$GATE_PASS" | openssl passwd -apr1 -stdin)
printf '%s:%s\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$hash" > auth/htpasswd

echo "Gate user: $GATE_EMAIL"
echo "Gate secret (shown once, store it in your manager now):"
printf '%s\n' "$GATE_PASS"
echo
echo "Set GRIST_ADMIN_EMAIL to $GATE_EMAIL in the compose .env, or the gate will let you in"
echo "as a user who is not the installation administrator."
```

## Proving the gate is real

Run this once the deploy reports ready. A gate you have not tested is a gate you are guessing
about, and the failure mode is an instance where every visitor is the owner.

Step 4 is not decoration. It is the step that caught the Authorization-header bug on the first real
run of this recipe, in a deploy where steps 1 to 3 all passed.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prove the Grist gate is in front, cannot be bypassed by a spoofed header, and identifies you.
#   GATE_EMAIL=you@example.com GATE_SECRET=[REDACTED:value] ./verify-grist.sh grist-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = gated and working, 1 = NOT gated, 2 = inconclusive (it may still be starting).
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: verify-grist.sh <host>}"
: "${GATE_EMAIL:?set GATE_EMAIL to the email you deployed with}"
: "${GATE_SECRET:[REDACTED:value] GATE_SECRET to the gate secret}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE THE WHOLE SCRIPT ON PROOF THAT GRIST IS ANSWERING. Everything below is vacuous
#    against an error page, and redu's hostname answers 502 for the first minutes.
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/status" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/status")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Re-run; this is NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -q "is alive" "$TMP/status"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /status returned 200 but not Grist's own body." >&2
  echo "  Something else is answering on this hostname. Do not read this as gated." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# 2. Anonymous must be refused. 401 is the POSITIVE result here, not a problem.
anon=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$anon" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: an anonymous request to / answered $anon, expected 401." >&2
  echo "The gate is not in front of Grist. Anyone loading this URL is already the administrator." >&2
  echo "Do not leave this instance running." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 3. And it must not be bypassable by sending the trusted header yourself.
spoof=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
  -H "X-Forwarded-User: someone-else@example.org" "https://$HOST/")
if [ "$spoof" != "401" ]; then
  echo "FAIL: a request carrying its own X-Forwarded-User answered $spoof, expected 401." >&2
  echo "nginx is not overwriting the header, so identity is client-controlled." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# 4. The positive half, which is what proves the two 401s above mean anything at all:
#    with the gate credentials, Grist must report YOU as the signed-in user.
#    A 401 HERE, with steps 1-3 passing, is the Authorization-header bug: nginx is forwarding
#    the basic-auth credentials and Grist is rejecting them as a malformed API key. Confirm with
#    `curl -u "$GATE_EMAIL:$GATE_SECRET" https://$HOST/api/profile/user`, which prints
#    "unsupported Authorization scheme, expected 'Bearer'". Fix: proxy_set_header Authorization "".
printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$GATE_EMAIL" "$GATE_SECRET" > "$TMP/curlrc"
me=$(curl -sS -K "$TMP/curlrc" -o "$TMP/me" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/profile/user")
if [ "$me" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: authenticated /api/profile/user answered $me." >&2
  echo "  A 404 means the endpoint moved: probe for the live route rather than assuming this one," >&2
  echo "  and do not read a 404 as a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi
if ! grep -qi "$GATE_EMAIL" "$TMP/me"; then
  echo "FAIL: authenticated, but Grist does not report $GATE_EMAIL as the user." >&2
  echo "The forward-auth header is not reaching Grist. Check GRIST_FORWARD_AUTH_HEADER." >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "OK: /status alive, anonymous 401, spoofed header 401, Grist reports $GATE_EMAIL."
echo "Two things left for a human: open a document and check a formula evaluates (that is the"
echo "Python sandbox), and confirm /persist is a mounted volume, not container-local disk."
```

## The three that actually break it

**No login system.** Covered above, and it is the reason for the second container. A single-container
Grist on a public URL hands ownership to whoever loads it.

**The database that is not your data.** Postgres holds accounts, orgs and metadata. Your actual
documents are `.grist` files under `/persist/docs`. Without the volume, a redeploy leaves a Grist
that lists everything and has nothing.

**The sandbox default.** Formulas are Python, and grist-core defaults to running them unsandboxed
inside the container. `GRIST_SANDBOX_FLAVOR=gvisor` uses the runsc that the official image already
ships, and it fails loudly if it cannot.
